Ah, so consumers decide what the minimum wage should be and the shareholders what the top wage should be?

Consumers decide what the natural maximum wage should be (if prices climb too high they stop buying) and labourers decide what the natural minimum wage should be (if wages fall too low it's not worth their while to turn up). The same is true of any good or service in a free market, labour is no different,

With government jobs the state decides what the natural maximum wage should be, or the workers decide via public unions (if they've achieved regulatory capture). Either way the consumer (the taxpayer) has to pay or borrow to cover the costs no matter what their actual demand is. The natural minimum wage is still determined by the labour pool unless it's forced labour in which case the state decides.

There's a really good video about the importance of pricing here. Just replace "steel" with "labour."
Ok, so in a free market those who control the flow of information set the prize?

All prices in a free market are a result of negotiation between consumers and providers. The "flow" of information isn't really controlled by anyone, it's just the product of everyone's actions added together.

For example, imagine you're a miller producing refined flour. Now imagine that people start a trend towards buying brown bread instead of white because they think it's healthier. The result of that is that the supermarkets will sell less white bread, which means they'll make less purchasing orders for white bread from the bakers, who'll buy less white flour next month from you. So you'll know to produce less white flour and sell off your inventory at a lower price. It also means that the price of brown flour will rise, so you'll know to invest in unrefined milling equipment.

The beauty of it is, no one ever has to know what's going on throughout the whole system; even if you're separated from the end consumer by a hundred or a thousand steps you still only need to know about one step above and one step below you.

This is how traders in Scandinavia traded for silk with merchants in China back before either of them even knew the other civilisation existed. No one organised the silk road or surveyed Norse farmers to find out how much they liked silk, it was just one long chain of people offering each other stuff in exchange for stuff they thought someone else would want more.
